soil-env-159.title: Methane from waterlogged thaw and Arctic lakes
soil-env-159.text: Methanogenesis, the making of methane by microbes, needs ground with no oxygen at all. So permafrost methane centres on Arctic lakes, where 2022 observations show at least half of the methane made reaches the air. How much thaw will yield is still a matter of debate. A 2015 review found sites without oxygen emitted 75–85% less than sites with it. Yet a 2018 incubation study found methane matched CO2 once methane-making microbes were established. Most of the carbon is young. A 2017 paper found less than 10% of methane from thawing peatlands came from old, thawed carbon, the rest from decay of modern carbon. Peatland methane after thaw starts high, at 82 milligrams per square meter per day, then falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

soil-env-215.title: Arctic methane and a feedback still taking shape
soil-env-215.text: Arctic-Boreal lands release about 48.7 Tg of methane a year, a 2024 assessment found, and marine sources add about 4.9 Tg. The gas comes mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, the breakdown of clathrates and the melting Greenland ice sheet. Clathrates are icy solids that trap gas inside, and they hold about 20 Gt of permafrost-associated methane. Permafrost itself holds almost twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. The emissions form a positive climate feedback. Thaw exposes organic material to methanogenesis, and methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Thermokarst lakes are frequent sources, and at least half the methane made in them reaches the atmosphere. Radiocarbon dating suggests 0.2 to 2.5 Pg of permafrost carbon was released as methane and CO2 over the last 60 years. The future pace is debated, as {{ref:soil-env-159}} showed. A 2015 review found anaerobic thaw sites, those without oxygen, emitted 75-85% less in total than aerobic ones. A 2018 seven-year incubation found methane production matched CO2 once methanogenic microbes became established. For now, no evidence ties the Arctic to the methane rise since about 2018, which points instead to tropical wetlands. Its role, though, will very likely grow.

soil-env-161.title: Putting numbers on permafrost's future emissions
soil-env-161.text: Early estimates missed the fast route. Preliminary 2011 analyses put permafrost emissions at around 15% of human emissions, but they could not account for {{ref:soil-env-160}}. A 2020 study looked at northern permafrost peatlands, 3.7 of the 18 million km2. It found they would cause ~1% of human radiative forcing, the extra warming push from greenhouse gases, by 2100, and become net carbon sinks within 200 years. A 2021 estimate that included sudden collapse gave 150–200 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2100 at 1.5 °C of warming. It gave 220–300 at 2 °C and 400–500 above 4 °C. A 2022 assessment found that this fast thaw adds 50% to gradual rates, or 14 billion tons of CO2 equivalent by 2100 per degree of warming.

soil-env-149.title: Pereletok, the frost that outlasts a summer
soil-env-149.text: The Russian word pereletok means that which survives over the summer. It names a layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws, also called intergelisol. Some schemes split frozen ground into permafrost, pereletok and seasonally frozen ground by how long it stays frozen. Pereletok can be seen as part of the active layer that stays frozen after an unusually cool summer or cold winter. Its boundary with permafrost has no universal definition and is hard to draw in the field.

soil-env-148.title: How soils form in the thin layer that thaws
soil-env-148.text: Above permafrost, the ground churns itself. Cryoturbation, mixing by freezing and thawing, dominates soil formation in the active layer and tends to make it uniform. Yet these soils still vary markedly with their parent rock, because weathering is so slow in the very cold climate. Decay is slow too. That makes gelisols, the permafrost soils, an important sink for carbon dioxide. The same stored carbon is a hazard. Permafrost thaw may accelerate global warming, especially if the carbon predates the recent glacial maxima.

soil-env-172.title: Black carbon, the charcoal hidden in soil
soil-env-172.text: The terra preta soils of central Amazonia average three times more soil organic matter than the soils around them. They are rich in black carbon: charcoal particles and soot from vegetation fires or deposited from the air. Black carbon typically makes up 1 to 6% of the organic carbon stored in soils, and up to 60%. In tropical soils it serves as a reservoir of nutrients, and soils without much of it are significantly less fertile. Slash-and-burn farming adds black carbon to soil. Slash-and-char would add it while avoiding high emissions of CO2 and volatile black carbon.

soil-env-160.title: Abrupt thaw, when frozen hillsides collapse in days
soil-env-160.text: In 2020 a heatwave struck Siberia. Afterward, thaw slumps on the northern Taymyr Peninsula rose 17-fold, from 82 to 1404, and the soil carbon they mobilized rose 28-fold. This is abrupt permafrost thaw. Hillsides collapse in retrogressive thaw slumps, and thermokarst lakes form, exposing deep soil to microbes within days. Climate models long focused on gradual thaw, because the abrupt kind is hard to model. Some sites have not waited for the models. In 2019, three permafrost sites expected to stay frozen for 70 more years under the intermediate RCP4.5 pathway had already thawed abruptly. The stakes are large. Abrupt thaw adds between 60 and 100 gigatonnes of carbon by 2300, raising emissions by ~125–190% over gradual thaw alone. It often raises methane's share relative to carbon dioxide, a major source of uncertainty in projections of permafrost methane. In peatlands, methane after thaw starts high, 82 milligrams per square metre per day, but falls nearly threefold as the bog matures.

soil-env-151.title: The unfrozen gap that warming opens above permafrost
soil-env-151.text: Sometimes ground that thaws in summer fails to refreeze in winter. An unfrozen layer then opens between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost below: a supra-permafrost talik. Ordinary taliks are usually tied to lakes and rivers, but this one results from climate warming. It forms in moderately cold regions. Colder regions simply thaw deeper in summer, and warm, shallow permafrost just disappears. As air temperature or snow depth rises, the talik thickens until the deep permafrost vanishes. This type of talik has recently been observed in Russia.

soil-env-115.title: The compost bomb, a proposed runaway in peat
soil-env-115.text: Microbes release heat as they decompose organic matter, yet climate models do not account for it. A 2011 study identified a possible consequence, the compost-bomb instability. It is a proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands. The authors noted that for any fixed atmospheric temperature, soil carbon has a unique stable equilibrium. Peatlands are predicted to shift from carbon sink to source this century. Even so, they are still left out of the main Earth system models.

soil-env-214.title: Carbon cycle feedbacks, mostly on the side of cooling
soil-env-214.text: So far, Earth's carbon cycle has mostly worked against warming. Land and ocean sinks absorb around half of current emissions. That fraction could rise to three-quarters if emissions fall, or drop to one-third by 2100 if they rise. If emissions stay very high after this century, land ecosystems would become a net carbon source. Some processes push back. Through CO2 fertilization, more carbon dioxide raises plant productivity, and plants lose less water through their stomata, the pores in their leaves. Over the geological long term, chemical weathering removes CO2, and current warming is increasing it.

soil-env-126.title: How weathering rock pulls carbon from the sky
soil-env-126.text: Rain slowly scrubs carbon dioxide from the air. Rain and groundwater carry carbonic acid, which dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals and removes CO2 from the atmosphere. In theory, silicate weathering sequesters 1 mol of CO2 for each mol of Ca2+ or Mg2+ released, though natural ratios vary with temperature and CO2 pressure. The dissolved bicarbonate travels through soil and groundwater to the ocean, where organisms build carbonate shells. Over geological time this is thought to stabilize climate. Carbonate weathering followed by carbonate precipitation sequesters no net CO2. The reactions also reverse when carbonate meets acids, as in soils. Liming acid soil neutralizes hydrogen ions but releases CO2 from the limestone.

soil-env-125.title: Enhanced weathering: crushed rock as a carbon trap
soil-env-125.text: Crushed basalt spread on a field starts pulling carbon dioxide from the air. Enhanced weathering speeds up the natural weathering of {{ref:soil-env-126}} by grinding silicate rock fine so that it reacts with water and air. Through carbonic acid it removes CO2 and stores it permanently, in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity. Methods are land-based, such as in-situ carbonation of silicates, or ocean-based. Ultramafic rock could store hundreds to thousands of years' worth of CO2 emissions. Mine tailings and alkaline industrial wastes such as steel slag or biomass ash could serve first, though more basalt mining might eventually be needed. Crushed rock mixed into soil can also benefit plant health when calcium or magnesium is present. In July 2020 a group of scientists judged that spreading finely crushed basalt on fields has potential for national carbon dioxide removal. A 2020 analysis put its cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2. That compares with US$100–200 for BECCS, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage, and US$100–300 for direct air capture. Overall it could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year, with cost estimates in the US$50–200 per tonne range.

soil-env-128.title: Mineral carbonation, turning rock and CO2 into stone
soil-env-128.text: In 1990 Seifritz proposed locking carbon dioxide into rock on purpose. Mineral carbonation dissolves silicate minerals and turns them into carbonate, which holds the CO2. Lackner and colleagues and the Albany Research Center developed the idea. Early work reacted crushed silicates in reactors at about 180 °C and 15 MPa of CO2. In-situ methods instead inject CO2 into silicate rock formations. Research has mostly targeted CO2 from flue gas, the exhaust of furnaces and boilers. Using CO2 taken from the air instead, it could serve as geoengineering. Soil remineralization with crushed rock contributes to the same process of enhanced weathering.

soil-env-127.title: Spreading rock dust on land and the questions it raises
soil-env-127.text: Crushed silicate rock spread over the ground does not dissolve at a fixed speed. In this land version of enhanced weathering, the rate depends on the rock's reactive surface area, the pH and buffer capacity of the soil, and soil biological activity. It remains uncertain. That uncertainty drives the costs. Grinding takes energy, and how much depends on how quickly the rock dissolves. A 2012 study found a wide range of possible costs, mostly because dissolution rates are uncertain. Water is the other open question. Weathering slows as the soil solution saturates, so some researchers argue low rainfall limits it. Others say new minerals or plant uptake keep it going.

soil-env-122.title: How root fungi build crumbs that guard carbon
soil-env-122.text: Soil aggregates, crumbs of particles stuck together, shield organic carbon from soil microbes. So more aggregates can mean more stored carbon, and mycorrhizal fungi help build them. Much evidence shows that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi increase aggregate formation, possibly through the protein glomalin. Even if glomalin itself decays readily, it may still store carbon by promoting aggregates that protect other organic matter. Ectomycorrhizal fungi are another story. Their only links to aggregation are anecdotal, from sand bags, with no evidence yet that they aid aggregates in field soils.

soil-env-124.title: When root fungi starve the decomposers
soil-env-124.text: In 1971, researchers in New Zealand's Pinus radiata plantations excluded roots and their fungi from the soil, and the soil lost carbon on net. It was the first report of a surprising effect. Ectomycorrhizal fungi can slow decomposition by competing with free-living decomposers for nutrients or water. Several later studies found these fungi reduce decomposer activity and so increase soil carbon storage. A theoretical model shows one route. Fungal access to organic nitrogen should slow decomposition by leaving decomposers short of nutrients. Koide and Wu argued in 2003 that competition for soil water may matter more than competition for nutrients.

soil-env-123.title: When root fungi feed the decomposers instead
soil-env-123.text: Mycorrhizal fungi can also speed up decay. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi have been shown to increase soil carbon decomposition in nutrient-rich patches. They are thought to lack the enzymes to do this themselves. Instead, they are believed to stimulate free-living decomposers by exuding easily used carbon compounds, a form of the priming effect. In lab experiments, soils with arbuscular fungi lose more carbon than soils without them, and the gap widens under elevated CO2. For ectomycorrhizal fungi the evidence is inconclusive. Field data suggest faster carbon loss, but lab tests show root exudation, the release of compounds from roots, falls as ectomycorrhizal colonization rises.

soil-env-121.title: Do tough fungal tissues keep carbon in the soil
soil-env-121.text: How slowly a fungus rots may decide how long its carbon stays underground. Glomalin, made only by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, accumulates in some soils and may be a substantial share of their carbon. Its importance is now disputed. Later experiments found that arbuscular fungi cause net soil carbon losses. Protein analysis showed that most proteins extracted as glomalin are not mycorrhizal at all, so its role is likely overestimated. Ectomycorrhizal tissue had its own suspect, chitin, long thought to slow decay. In 2012 Fernandez and Koide found that it does not decompose more slowly than other compounds.

reviews.soil-carbon-and-climate: Soils hold about 2,700 Gt of carbon, roughly three times the carbon in the atmosphere, and about 60 GtC a year flows into them and back out again. Warming tilts that balance, because warmer soils respire and decompose faster, while tillage and land clearing have already stripped much soil organic carbon. The largest frozen store, northern permafrost, holds about twice the carbon of the atmosphere, and as the active layer deepens, gradual and abrupt thaw let microbes release it as carbon dioxide and methane. Not every feedback runs toward warming. Plants, mycorrhizal fungi, peatlands and slow rock weathering draw carbon down, and practices from carbon farming to wetland restoration and enhanced weathering aim to strengthen them.
